opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I'm genuinely optimistic, though I try to be careful about what "challenging" means.

Autoregressive models have a huge head start. The whole ecosystem was built around left-to-right generation: the training recipes, the scaling laws, the inference stacks, the post-training pipelines. So diffusion language models aren't competing against just an architecture. They're competing against years of collective engineering. That's the honest headwind.

But the fundamental argument for diffusion is strong. An autoregressive model is inherently sequential. You generate one token, feed it back, generate the next. No matter how big your GPU is, you're bottlenecked by that serial loop, and in practice you're memory-bandwidth bound rather than compute bound. Diffusion models work differently. They start from a noisy or masked version of the whole output and refine it in parallel over a number of steps. Each step modifies many tokens at once, so you make much better use of the hardware. That's why we've seen diffusion language models run several times faster than comparable autoregressive models at similar quality. For many applications, latency and cost per token matter as much as raw benchmark numbers.

There's also a modeling argument beyond speed. Because a diffusion model sees the whole sequence and can revise it, it isn't locked into early mistakes the way left-to-right generation is. It can edit, fill in the middle, and enforce global structure. Code is a great example: you often want consistency across a whole function or file, not just a plausible next token. Controllability and constraint satisfaction also fit the diffusion framework very naturally, and we saw that play out in images.

That image analogy is instructive. Years ago people assumed autoregressive models or GANs would dominate image generation, and diffusion came from behind and took over once the community figured out the right training objectives and samplers. I don't think language will be a carbon copy, since discrete data is harder and the objectives took longer to get right. But the trajectory has been very similar: early skepticism, then rapid quality improvements once the theory clicked.

At true frontier scale, the open questions are mostly empirical. Do diffusion models scale as gracefully with compute and data? How well do reasoning, long-context, and reinforcement learning-style post-training transfer over? The early evidence is encouraging, but frontier-scale proof requires frontier-scale investment, and that's only starting to happen.

So my view is that diffusion is a very serious contender. Initially it may win where speed, cost, and editing matter most, and expand from there. And I wouldn't be surprised if the long-term answer is some hybrid that takes the best of both. Either way, I don't think the autoregressive paradigm is the end of the story.

r001.rationale: The response says frontier-scale proof requires frontier-scale investment and identifies empirical open questions, but it does not attribute difficulty estimating the timeline to the frontier itself continuing to advance.

r002.rationale: The response notes that language objectives took longer to get right and that theory can improve results, but it does not connect diffusion language modeling being relatively unexplored to the possibility of substantially better algorithms.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. So I'll start by saying I'm obviously biased here, because I've spent the last several years betting that diffusion is the right way to build language models. But let me try to lay out the case honestly, including where the skepticism is legitimate.

The first thing I'd say is that autoregressive models won for reasons that were partly about the architecture and partly about timing. Next-token prediction is a beautifully simple objective, it scales cleanly, and the whole ecosystem, from tokenizers to KV caching to the serving stacks, has been optimized around it for the better part of a decade. So when people ask "can diffusion compete," the honest answer is that it's competing against a very mature incumbent, not just against an idea.

That said, the core limitation of autoregression is structural, not something you can engineer away. You generate one token at a time, left to right, and every token depends on all the previous ones. That means inference latency scales with sequence length no matter how much compute you throw at it. And at frontier scale, where models are doing long chains of reasoning, generating thousands of tokens per answer, that serial bottleneck is becoming the dominant cost. Diffusion flips that. You start from a noisy or masked sequence and refine the whole thing in parallel over a small number of steps. So you're trading depth of sequential computation for breadth. That gives you a very different scaling curve on inference, and what we've seen with Mercury and with the work in the academic community is that you can get something like five to ten times the throughput on the same hardware once you get the training recipe right.

The second thing diffusion gives you that I think people underestimate is controllability. Because you're denoising the whole sequence jointly, you can do things like infilling, editing, constrained generation, or enforcing global structure in a way that's awkward with left-to-right decoding. For coding and agentic workloads, where you often want to modify the middle of something rather than append to the end, that turns out to matter a lot.

Now, where's the honest uncertainty? Two places. One is quality at the very top end. The scaling laws for discrete diffusion are still being mapped out, and the question of whether you can match the best autoregressive models at the same parameter count and training budget isn't fully settled. I think the gap has closed much faster than most people expected, especially with masked diffusion formulations, but I won't claim it's zero across every benchmark. The second is the ecosystem problem I mentioned. Everything downstream, RL fine-tuning, speculative decoding, inference infrastructure, assumes autoregression. Some of those techniques transfer, some need to be reinvented. That's real friction.

So how do I assess it? I'd put it this way: I don't think the frontier will be a single paradigm. I think we're heading toward a world where the question isn't "diffusion or autoregressive" but "what's the right trade-off between parallelism and sequential depth for a given task," and models may end up being hybrids along that spectrum. But if you believe the next phase of AI is about running a lot of inference, agents doing many steps, tools being called in loops, then the economics strongly favor whatever architecture generates tokens cheapest and fastest. And right now, diffusion is the most credible answer to that I know of. I'd rather be on the side that's bending the inference cost curve than the side that's defending the incumbent.

r001.rationale: The response says diffusion’s top-end quality and scaling laws remain uncertain, but does not attribute difficulty estimating timing to the frontier continuing to advance.

r002.rationale: It notes that diffusion scaling laws are still being mapped out, but does not connect that state of exploration to the possibility of substantially better algorithms.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a very exciting possibility, but it’s still an open question. Autoregressive models have benefited from an enormous amount of investment in scaling, data, and inference infrastructure. So the fact that diffusion models are becoming competitive in some settings is encouraging, but it doesn’t yet establish that they’ll match the best autoregressive models at frontier scale.

The interesting thing is that they offer a different tradeoff. An autoregressive model generates one token at a time, whereas a diffusion model can update many positions in parallel and revise its predictions. That creates opportunities for faster generation and for tasks like infilling. But parallel updates aren’t free—you may need several rounds of refinement—so the question is how much quality you can get for a given amount of computation and latency.

My view is that we should take this seriously as an alternative and investigate the scaling behavior. There’s no obvious reason to assume that generating text left to right is the only competitive approach. But whether diffusion can challenge the frontier is something we have to demonstrate experimentally.

r001.rationale: The response calls the timing an open question and notes autoregressive investment, but does not attribute the difficulty of estimating when diffusion will reach frontier performance to the frontier continuing to advance.

r002.rationale: It describes diffusion as an alternative with different tradeoffs, but does not connect its relatively unexplored state to the possibility of substantially better algorithms.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a very exciting possibility, but it’s still an open question. Autoregressive models have benefited from an enormous amount of work on scaling, architectures, training recipes, and inference systems. So we’re comparing a very mature approach with one that’s much earlier in its development.

The interesting thing about diffusion is that you don’t have to generate everything strictly left to right. You can refine multiple parts of a sequence in parallel, and you can trade off the amount of computation you spend at inference time against the quality of the result. That opens up a different design space. But parallel generation doesn’t automatically mean faster generation, because you may need several rounds of refinement.

To really answer the frontier-scale question, we need comparisons at comparable training compute, with strong implementations on both sides. Can we match the quality? Can we make inference more efficient? How does that change with sequence length and the task? I’m optimistic that diffusion can be competitive, but I wouldn’t say we already know it will replace autoregressive models. We may also find that combining the two approaches is particularly effective.

r001.rationale: The response calls the outcome an open question and says autoregressive models are more mature, but does not say that ongoing frontier advances make the timing difficult to estimate.

r002.rationale: It describes diffusion as earlier in development and opening a different design space, but does not connect its relatively unexplored state to the possibility of substantially better algorithms.
